claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo contains approximately 20 at.% each of Nb, Zr, Ti, Hf, and Mo.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered single-phase BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has limited room-temperature compressive plasticity.
Replacing part of the Mo with Zr will narrow the alloy's electronegativity-difference distribution.
Replacing part of the Mo with Zr will reduce local atomic-scale lattice distortion.
A suitable partial replacement of Mo by Zr can retain the disordered single-phase BCC structure.
Reduced electronegativity mismatch and lattice strain will facilitate dislocation motion.
Easier dislocation motion will increase room-temperature compressive plastic deformation.
Solid-solution strengthening is responsible for the high yield strength of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
Partial Mo replacement can improve plasticity without significantly compromising solid-solution strengthening.
The modified alloys will exhibit a statistically significant increase in room-temperature compressive plastic strain.
The modified alloys will retain yield strength close to 1719 MPa, with no more than a 15% reduction.
The plasticity benefit is conditional on retaining a disordered single-phase BCC structure.
Excessive Mo reduction may produce phase separation or intermetallic phases.
Substitution by elements with excessive atomic-size or bonding dissimilarity may produce phase separation or intermetallic phases.

contradictions.description: The boundary treats formation of secondary phases after excessive substitution as an anticipated condition outside the hypothesis's valid range, whereas the falsification rule treats detection of any such phases as falsifying the hypothesis. A failed high-substitution specimen would therefore both satisfy the stated boundary and count as falsification.
